callouts.label: Prospect View
callouts.hint: Find the tall glass pane on the far left that looks out over a lake, rolling hills, and a distant tree line with nothing blocking the view.
callouts.description: Prospect is an unblocked view over a distance (Terrapin Bright Green, group: Nature of the Space). It feels open and gives a sense of safety and control. Low partitions, glass, and open floor plans protect it. When the view includes greenery or sky it also supports Visual Connection with Nature.
callouts.tip: Seat people where they can see out, not just where the layout is easiest.

callouts.label: Daylight and Shadow
callouts.hint: Find the warm, slanted shaft of sunlight leaving the big window, with leaf-shaped dappled shadows where it lands on the floor.
callouts.description: Dynamic and Diffuse Light is light and shadow that change over time, as they do outdoors (Terrapin, group: Nature in the Space). Chapter 19 gives the building-science side: side windows usefully light a room to about two times the window head height, and balancing glare, heat loss, and overheating is part of the job.

callouts.label: Plants and Greenery
callouts.hint: Find the tall panel of layered green leaves, ferns, and trailing vines covering the middle of the back wall.
callouts.description: Plants are a direct visual connection with nature: a view to living systems and natural processes (Terrapin, group: Nature in the Space). The pattern is about the experience of living things. Plants need light, watering, and drainage, so the interior, lighting, and moisture plans have to be designed for them from the start.

callouts.label: Wood and Natural Materials
callouts.hint: Find the warm golden wall of upright oak slats with clearly visible grain lines and a few knots.
callouts.description: Material Connection with Nature uses lightly processed materials that reflect the local ecology or geology, such as wood and stone (Terrapin, group: Natural Analogues). Chapter 20 covers regional lumber, renewable materials, and low-VOC finishes, which keep the warm look from bringing indoor air problems.
callouts.tip: Ask for the finish data sheet before you fall in love with the grain.

callouts.label: Biomorphic Forms
callouts.hint: Find the curving, leaf-veined room divider and the branching column that spreads into the ceiling like a tree.
callouts.description: Biomorphic Forms and Patterns are symbolic references to the contours, patterns, and textures found in nature (Terrapin, group: Natural Analogues). Nothing alive is present. A screen cut in a leaf-vein pattern or a column that branches like a tree works as an analogue, so it is design choice rather than a systems requirement.

callouts.label: Breeze and Airflow
callouts.hint: Find the low window on the left standing open, with a pale curtain curling inward in the moving air.
callouts.description: Thermal and Airflow Variability means subtle changes in air temperature, humidity, and air movement across the skin, like the outdoors (Terrapin, group: Nature in the Space). Operable windows give people control. Chapter 4 lists air speed among the factors of thermal comfort, and Chapters 11 and 12 remind us that a closed window must also be airtight.

callouts.label: Water Feature
callouts.hint: Find the low stone basin on the floor with a thin trickling stream, ripples, and a few smooth pebbles.
callouts.description: Presence of Water enhances a place through seeing, hearing, or touching water (Terrapin, group: Nature in the Space). A gentle trickle can calm or stimulate. It is also a moisture source: Chapter 4 explains why added humidity has to be matched with ventilation and with surfaces warmer than the dew point.

callouts.label: Daylight Versus Electric Light
callouts.hint: Find the wide strip along the bottom comparing two versions of the same room: one with sunlit windows and dimmed ceiling lights, the other with dark windows and every light blazing.
callouts.description: Daylight lowers lighting energy and cooling load, but only if the electric lighting responds. Daylight harvesting uses sensors to dim or switch off lights near windows (Chapter 19), connected through the lighting controls of Chapter 16. Daylight also varies with weather and season, so electric lighting still has to cover the dark hours.
callouts.tip: Daylight only saves energy when a sensor turns the lights down.

callouts.label: Mystery Path
callouts.hint: Find the curving pale floor inlay that bends behind a low screen toward a half-hidden doorway glowing with warm light.
callouts.description: Mystery is the promise of more information through partially hidden views that invite you to go deeper (Terrapin, group: Nature of the Space). A curving route, a screen with a gap, or a glimpse of light around a corner can create it. Good circulation still has to meet the egress and accessibility rules from Chapters 17 and 18.

callouts.label: Refuge Nook
callouts.hint: Find the cozy alcove on the right with a high-backed cushioned bench, a low ceiling over it, and a small reading lamp.
callouts.description: Refuge is a place for withdrawal, protected from behind and overhead, where a person can pull back from the main flow of activity (Terrapin, group: Nature of the Space). A window seat or reading nook can do it. Paired with a prospect view, it lets people see out while feeling sheltered.
